steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper that presents a new public benchmark dataset for basketball activity recognition recorded with wrist-worn inertial sensors. It should motivate why such a dataset is needed, say what the dataset contributes, and explain what impact it could have on HAR research.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- HAR and the state of public datasets (lab vs. in the wild)
- Sports as a semi-controlled recording environment
- Interest in IMU wearables for sports (research and industry)
- Contributions of the dataset
- Impact on the research community

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- HAR and public datasets
  - HAR: track physical movements, categorize into predefined classes/clusters; ML / deep learning classify sensor samples
  - survey: only 30 public datasets ever; 11 of 13 most cited released 2015 or prior
  - mostly lab-recorded, strict protocols; no solid annotation tools in the wild -> labs w/ cameras for labeling in hindsight
  - labeling labor-intensive -> few participants
  - hurdles in the wild -> imbalance: controlled vs uncontrolled datasets
- Sports = semi-controlled (e.g. Figure 1)
  - practice drills (controlled) + game sessions (uncontrolled)
  - highly variable, dynamic movements; high intraclass + intersubject variability (gender, height, weight, play style, athletic ability) [cite]
  - classifiers worse in the wild: weak labeling [cite], smoothness in performed activities [cite]
  - public sports dataset -> impact on design/validation of HAR algorithms; precise labels from video
- IMU wearables in sports
  - previous studies: Table 2 (sports), Table 3 (basketball), surveys [cite]
  - pro athletes use sensor-based training
  - Hannover 96, 1. FC Magdeburg use Vmaxpro (body-worn IMU; monitors movement, training recommendations incl. strength exercises via smartphone)
  - Adidas 2021: sensor inlay sole for soccer shoe, detects soccer-specific activities
  - SIQ (Finland) 2020: sensor basketball w/ feedback for shooting skills
- Contributions
  - first public sensor-based basketball dataset, teams doing structured drills + unstructured game
  - classes chosen by experienced players; full range of basketball activities
  - high dynamics, complexity, variability within/between subjects
  - warm-up, drill, game sessions -> mix of controlled/uncontrolled; game faster, more dynamic (other players)
  - no scoring info -> not for skill assessment; metadata: novice/expert; novices -> large variance
  - 24 participants (~two teams), two continents -> FIBA (Europe) vs NBA (Northern America) rule sets; unique
- Impact
  - Ubiquitous Computing community; no comparable (sports) dataset public: same activities, same hardware/modalities, controlled + uncontrolled
  - multi-part study, "free-movement" game; basketball easy to capture on video and label
  - new playground to benchmark, spot deficiencies in SOTA architectures
  - game phases: team/game dynamics -> group activity recognition
  - layered labels / multi-labels
  - open problems: Transfer Learning, Data Augmentation, complex activities in real-world settings; recording, annotation, preprocessing (segmentation), feature extraction, new DL methods, evaluation
  - commercial, mostly open-source setup (smartwatches + firmware); low-effort, deployable spontaneously, not restricted to basketball
  - labeling setup builds on community work, reproducibility

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Human activity recognition (HAR) systems try to track the physical movements of people and sort them into predefined activity classes or clusters. Machine learning methods, and especially deep learning, are used to classify samples of sensor data into these predefined classes. According to one survey, only 30 datasets in total have ever been publicly released and 11 of the 13 most cited datasets in the HAR community were released in 2015 or before. These datasets, especially the older ones, are usually recorded in labs and follow strict protocols for the activities and movement patterns. Scientists don't have solid annotation methods and tools for recordings in the wild, so they fall back to a controlled lab environment where visual systems, often cameras, can be set up to help label the sensor data afterwards. Labeling data is labor-intensive work, so the number of participants is often limited. Because there are significant hurdles for experiments in the wild, there are many more publicly available datasets from controlled environments than from uncontrolled environments.

Depending on how the experiment is designed, a sports environment, e.g. Figure 1, can however be seen as a semi-controlled environment, because the recording sessions can include practice drills, which are controlled, and also game sessions, which are uncontrolled. Because of the nature of sports, this data has highly variable and dynamic movement patterns. It has high intraclass variability and also high intersubject variability because of gender, height, weight, personal play style and athletic ability of the subject. These differences are important in real-world scenarios. In general classifiers perform worse on in-the-wild datasets than on datasets recorded in a lab, because of effects such as weak labeling or smoothness in the performed activities. So providing a publicly available dataset with complex sports-related activities can have an important impact on how we design and validate HAR algorithms in the future, and it gives researchers the security of a semi-controlled environment with precise labels that are based on video recordings.

Many previous studies, which are summarized in Table 2 (for sports), Table 3 (for basketball), and in earlier published surveys, show that there is interest in using wearable solutions based on inertial measurement units (IMUs) for activity recognition in sports. Professional athletes use sensor-based training methods to get better at their sport. The German professional soccer clubs Hannover 96 and 1. FC Magdeburg use Vmaxpro, a commercial body-worn IMU sensor, which monitors the movements of the athletes and shows training recommendations, including specific strength training exercises, on a smartphone for the trainer and the athlete. In 2021 Adidas, the sports fashion company, released an inlay sole for a soccer shoe that has a sensor in it, and it can detect soccer-specific activities. In the same way, in 2020 the Finnish company SIQ released a basketball with a sensor and feedback that aims to improve the shooting skills of players.

Contributions:
- first public sensor-based basketball dataset; teams doing structured drills + unstructured game
- classes selected by researchers with many years of basketball experience; full range of activities, key aspects of the sport
- high dynamics, complexity, variability within subject (execution style) and between subjects (experience, play style)
- warm-up, drill, game sessions -> mix of controlled and uncontrolled; game more dynamic, higher pace -> transition to semi-controlled
- no scoring info, so not necessarily for skill assessment; metadata has novice/expert; novices -> large variance
- 24 participants (~two complete teams), two continents -> FIBA in Europe vs NBA in Northern America rule sets; unique setup

Impact:
- for the Ubiquitous Computing community; no (sports) dataset of this scope/design public yet: same activities, same hardware and sensor modalities, controlled + uncontrolled
- multi-part study, "free-movement" game; basketball easy to capture in video and label in detail
- new playground to benchmark algorithms, spot deficiencies in SOTA architectures
- game phases model team/game dynamics -> group activity recognition in future studies
- layered labels / multi-labels
- open problems: Transfer Learning, Data Augmentation, complex activities in real-world environments; recording techniques, annotation, preprocessing (segmentation), feature extraction, DL methods, evaluation
- commercial, mostly open-source components (smartwatches + firmware); low-effort, deployable in spontaneous situations, not restricted to basketball
- labeling setup builds on previous community work, reproducibility

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Human activity recognition (HAR) systems try to track the physical movements of people and sort them into predefined activity classes or clusters. Machine learning methods, and especially deep learning, are used to classify samples of sensor data into these predefined classes. Scientists don't have solid annotation methods and tools for recordings in the wild, so they fall back to a controlled lab environment where visual systems, often cameras, can be set up to help label the sensor data afterwards. Labeling data is labor-intensive work, so the number of participants is often limited. Because there are significant hurdles for experiments in the wild, there are many more publicly available datasets from controlled environments than from uncontrolled environments.

Depending on how the experiment is designed, a sports environment, e.g. Figure 1, can however be seen as a semi-controlled environment, because the recording sessions can include practice drills, which are controlled, and also game sessions, which are uncontrolled. Because of the nature of sports, this data has highly variable and dynamic movement patterns. It has high intraclass variability and also high intersubject variability because of gender, height, weight, personal play style and athletic ability of the subject. These differences are important in real-world scenarios. In general classifiers perform worse on in-the-wild datasets than on datasets recorded in a lab, because of effects such as weak labeling or smoothness in the performed activities. So providing a publicly available dataset with complex sports-related activities can have an important impact on how we design and validate HAR algorithms in the future, and it gives researchers the security of a semi-controlled environment with precise labels that are based on video recordings.

Many previous studies, which are summarized in Table 2 (for sports), Table 3 (for basketball), and in earlier published surveys, show that there is interest in using wearable solutions based on inertial measurement units (IMUs) for activity recognition in sports. Professional athletes use sensor-based training methods to get better at their sport. The German professional soccer clubs Hannover 96 and 1. FC Magdeburg use Vmaxpro, a commercial body-worn IMU sensor, which monitors the movements of the athletes and shows training recommendations, including specific strength training exercises, on a smartphone for the trainer and the athlete. In 2021 Adidas, the sports fashion company, released an inlay sole for a soccer shoe that has a sensor in it, and it can detect soccer-specific activities. In the same way, in 2020 the Finnish company SIQ released a basketball with a sensor and feedback that aims to improve the shooting skills of players.

Contributions: This is the first publicly available dataset with sensor-based basketball activities that were collected from teams of players doing structured practice drills and also an unstructured game. The classes were selected by researchers who have many years of experience playing basketball, and they represent a full range of basketball activities that cover key aspects of the sport. The activities show high dynamics, complexity and variability within the same subject (because of different execution styles) and also between subjects (because of experience and play style). The recordings are split into warm-up, drill and game sessions, so the dataset has a mix of controlled and uncontrolled environments. The game is more dynamic because other players influence it and it has a higher pace than the drills. So this setup can be seen as a transition from a controlled environment to a semi-controlled recording environment. The dataset does not have information about successful scoring, so it is not necessarily meant to be used for skill assessment. But the metadata does have information about the experience of the players (novice or expert). Novices are players with little prior experience in playing basketball. So it can be expected that the way players execute activities has a large variance. The dataset was recorded from 24 participants (roughly two complete teams) on two continents, so it also includes the inherent differences between the rule sets of the International Basketball Federation (FIBA) in Europe and the National Basketball Association (NBA) in Northern America. This is a unique setup that is not available in other sports.

Impact: The Ubiquitous Computing community can use this dataset to tackle a variety of research questions in Human Activity Recognition. There is no publicly available (sports) dataset of this scope and study design yet, because this one has the same set of activities recorded with the same hardware and sensor modalities in both controlled and uncontrolled environments. The study has multiple parts, where some parts are controlled by prescribed activities and other parts are uncontrolled, like a "free-movement" game. Because of the nature of basketball, this mix of controlled conditions is easy to capture in video and to label manually in detail. The multi-part study makes the data more complex and diverse and gives researchers a new playground to benchmark algorithms and approaches and maybe to spot deficiencies in existing state-of-the-art architectures. Also, the game phases have data that models team and game dynamics, and future studies can explore this more deeply for group activity recognition. We provide layered labels, or multi-labels, because some activities consist of a series of other activities. The complex characteristics of the data and the differences because of the location can help with open research problems like Transfer Learning and Data Augmentation, and recognizing complex activities in dynamic and real-world environments. Further development in these areas may include, but is not restricted to, research on data recording techniques and annotation procedures, data preprocessing (e.g., data segmentation), feature extraction, or developing new deep learning methodologies and evaluation methods. For the methodology, we restricted our recording setup to commercial and mostly open-source recording components (especially the smartwatches and their firmware). This kind of low-effort recording setup has the big advantage that it can be deployed in spontaneous situations and, if it is developed further, it would not be restricted to basketball. The labeling setup builds on previous work by the community and focuses on reproducibility by other research labs.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Human activity recognition (HAR) systems aim to track people's physical movements and categorize them according to predefined activity classes or clusters. Methods from machine learning, and especially deep learning, are applied to classify samples of sensor data into predefined classes. According to [1], only 30 datasets in total have ever been released publicly and 11 out of the 13 most cited datasets in the HAR community were released in 2015 or prior. Such datasets, especially the older ones, are commonly recorded in laboratories and follow strict activity protocols and movement patterns. Since scientists lack solid annotation methods and tools for recordings in the wild, they tend to fall back to a controlled lab environment, in which visual systems, often cameras, can be installed to help label the sensor data in hindsight. Because labeling data is labor-intensive, the number of participants is often limited. Significant hurdles for experiments conducted in the wild lead to an imbalance between the number of publicly available datasets from controlled environments and from uncontrolled environments.

However, depending on the design of the experiment itself, a sports environment, e.g. Figure 1, can be seen as a semi-controlled environment, since its recording sessions can include both practice drills (controlled) and game sessions (uncontrolled). Due to the nature of the sports domain, this data contains highly variable and dynamic movement patterns, which exhibit high intraclass variability as well as high intersubject variability [2] due to the gender, height, weight, personal play style, and athletic ability of the subject. These differences are important in real-world scenarios, and classifiers generally perform worse on in-the-wild datasets than on lab-recorded datasets due to effects such as weak labeling [3] or smoothness in the performed activities [4]. Therefore, a publicly available dataset containing complex sports-related activities can have an important impact on how we design and validate future HAR algorithms, and gives researchers the security of a semi-controlled environment with precise labels based on video recordings.

Many previous studies, as summarized in Table 2 (for sports), Table 3 (for basketball), and earlier published surveys (e.g., [5,6]), show that there is an interest in using inertial measurement unit (IMU)-based wearable solutions for activity recognition in sports. Professional athletes use sensor-based training methods to improve their sporting skills. The German professional soccer clubs Hannover 96 and 1. FC Magdeburg use the commercial body-worn IMU sensors, Vmaxpro [7], which monitor the athletes' movements and present training recommendations, including specific strength training exercises, via smartphone for the trainer and athlete. In 2021, the sports fashion company Adidas released a sensor-equipped inlay sole for a soccer shoe [8], which can detect soccer-specific activities. Similarly, in 2020 the Finnish company SIQ [9] released a sensor-equipped basketball with feedback that aims to improve players' shooting skills.

Contributions: This dataset is the first publicly available dataset with sensor-based basketball activities collected from teams of players doing both structured practice drills and an unstructured game. The included classes were selected by researchers with many years of experience in playing basketball and represent a full range of basketball activities covering key aspects of the sport. The activities show high dynamics, complexity, and variability within the same subject (due to different execution styles) and between subjects (due to experience and play style). Since recordings are split into warm-up, drill, and game sessions, the dataset provides a mix of controlled and uncontrolled environments. The game shows a higher dynamic because of the influence of other players and a higher pace than the drills, so this setup can be seen as a transition from a controlled to a semi-controlled recording environment. Because the dataset does not contain information about successful scoring, it is not necessarily meant to be used for skill assessment. However, the metadata does contain information about the players' experience (novice or expert). Novices are players with little prior experience in playing basketball, so players' execution of activities can be expected to display a large variance. Since the dataset was recorded from 24 participants (roughly the size of two complete teams) across two continents, it also includes the inherent differences between the rule sets of the International Basketball Federation (FIBA) in Europe and the National Basketball Association (NBA) in Northern America. This unique setup is not available in other sports.

Impact: The Ubiquitous Computing community can use this dataset to tackle a variety of research questions in Human Activity Recognition. A (sports) dataset of this scope and study design is not yet publicly available, since it contains the same set of activities recorded with the same hardware and sensor modalities in both controlled and uncontrolled environments. The study is multi-part: some parts are controlled by prescribed activities and others are uncontrolled, such as a "free-movement" game. The nature of basketball is such that this mix of controlled conditions is easily captured in video and manually labeled in detail. The multi-part study adds complexity and diversity to the data and gives researchers a new playground to benchmark algorithms and approaches and (possibly) to spot deficiencies in existing state-of-the-art architectures. Furthermore, the game phases include data that models team and game dynamics, which future studies can explore more deeply with regard to group activity recognition. This work provides layered labels, or multi-labels, as certain activities consist of a series of other activities. The complex characteristics of the data and the differences due to location can help to address open research problems, such as Transfer Learning and Data Augmentation, and recognizing complex activities in dynamic and real-world environments. Further development in these areas may include, but is not restricted to, research on data recording techniques and annotation procedures, data preprocessing (e.g., data segmentation), feature extraction, or developing new deep learning methodologies and evaluation methods. Methodology-wise, we restricted our recording setup to commercial and mostly open-source recording components (in particular the smartwatches and their firmware). Such a low-effort recording setup has the significant advantage of being deployable in spontaneous situations and, if further developed, would not be restricted to basketball. The labeling setup builds on previous work by the community and focuses on reproducibility by other research labs.

References:

[2] Mitchell et al. (2013) Mitchell, E.; Monaghan, D.; O’Connor, N.E. Classification of sporting activities using smartphone accelerometers. Sensors 2013 , 13 , 5317–5337.
